Surah 32: As-Sajdah

(Meccan, and it has thirty verses; it is said twenty-nine.)

﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ Either it is the name of the surah, in which case its position (mahall) is in the nominative case, as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: this is named "Alif Lam Mim." The indication of it (by a demonstrative) before the mention of it has come, you already know its secret. Or it is recited in the manner of enumeration (ta'did), in which case it has no position (mahall) in terms of i'rab (grammatical case-analysis).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 2:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it, is from the Lord of the worlds﴾

﴿The revelation of the Book﴾ — according to the first view, it is a predicate following a predicate, on the basis that it is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the sense of the object (maf'ul) for emphasis (mubalaghah). According to the second view, it is a predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "the composition of the kind mentioned is the revelation of the Book." It has also been said that it is the predicate of "Alif-Lam-Mim," i.e., "the one named by it is the revelation of the Book." It has been mentioned repeatedly that what is made the title of a subject should be something whose attribution to it is already known beforehand; and since there is no prior familiarity with the naming, its proper function is to inform of it. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ is a third predicate according to the first view, and a second predicate according to the last two. It has also been said that it is a predicate of "the revelation of the Book," so His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ is connected to an implied element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the genitive position, i.e., "existing from Him, exalted is He," not to "revelation" (tanzil), because a verbal noun does not govern what comes after the predicate. The most suitable view then is that it is the predicate, and "there is no doubt in it" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the Book" or a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad), and the pronoun in "fihi" refers to the content of the whole sentence, as if it were said: there is no doubt in that, i.e., in its being sent down from the Lord of the worlds. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 3:

﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"?﴾ Their saying this is a denial on their part that it is from the Lord of the worlds. Therefore its subject (mawrid) must be a predicate intended for its own sake (hukman maqsud al-ifada), not a qualifier of a predicate, namely the negation of doubt concerning it. This was refuted for them and nullified, when the disjunctive "am" (am al-munqati'a, "or" introducing a new statement) was used, as a denial of it and an expression of wonder at it, because of how plainly its falsehood is evident and the impossibility of its being fabricated. Then he turned from it to explaining the truth of what they denied, when it was said: ﴿Rather, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, with the name of the Lord being attached to his pronoun (ﷺ) after it had previously been attached to "the worlds," as an honouring of him (ﷺ). Then this was further confirmed by explaining its purpose, when it was said: ﴿That you may warn a people to whom no warner has come before you, that they may be guided﴾. The explanation of the purpose and wisdom of a thing, especially when the purpose is a praiseworthy one that brings about noble benefits at a time of great need for it, is among the things that establish the existence of the thing and inevitably confirm it. Indeed, the Quraysh were among the most astray of people and the most in need of guidance, through the sending of a Messenger and the revelation of the Book, since no messenger had been sent to them (p-80) before him (ﷺ), i.e., no warner had come to them before your warning, or before your time. The expectation (al-tarajji) is considered on his part (ﷺ), i.e., that you warn them while hoping for their guidance, or in hope of their being guided. Know that what has been mentioned of confirmation applies only on the basis of what has been mentioned, that the revelation of the Book is a fresh beginning (mubtada'an). As for the other possibilities, there is no confirmation at all, because His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ is a fourth predicate on the first reading, and a third predicate on the last two readings. In any case, its being from the Lord of the worlds is a judgment intended for its own sake, not a qualifier of another judgment, so reflect upon this.

Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then settled Himself upon the Throne. Its explanation has passed earlier.

﴿You have, besides Him, no protector or intercessor.﴾ That is: if you transgress beyond His pleasure, you have no one who will help you, intercede for you, or protect you from His punishment. That is, apart from Him, you have no "protector or intercessor"; rather, He is the One who takes charge of your affairs and gives you victory in the situations where victory is sought. Moreover, the intercessor (shafi') is, metaphorically, an expression for the helper (nasir). So if He forsakes you, you will have no protector or helper.

﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾ That is: will you not hear these admonitions so that you take heed from them? Or: do you hear them and yet not take heed from them? The reproach in the first reading is directed at both the failure to hear and the failure to take heed together; in the second, it is directed at the failure to take heed despite the realization of what hearing requires.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 5:

﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth﴾. It is said: He arranges the affair of the worldly life through heavenly causes, from the angels and others, whose effects and rulings descend to the earth.

﴿Then it ascends to Him﴾, i.e., He establishes in His knowledge [the affair] as existing in actuality, ﴿in a Day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count﴾, i.e., in a lengthy span of time. The purpose is to explain the great extent of the duration between the arranging of events and their occurrence in time. It is also said: He arranges the affair of daily events by recording them in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), whereupon He sends down the angels with them. Then [the affair] ascends to Him in a time that is like a thousand years of what you count, for the distance between the heaven and the earth is a journey of five hundred years. It is also said: He decrees a decree of a thousand years, so the angel descends with it, then it ascends after the thousand [years] for another thousand. It is also said: He arranges the affair of the whole world until the Hour (qiyam al-sa'ah) comes, and then the entire affair ascends to Him at its establishment. It is also said: He arranges what is commanded of acts of obedience, sent down from heaven to earth by revelation, and then it does not ascend to Him in its purity except after a lengthy period, because of the scarcity of the sincere and of purely sincere deeds. And you know that the scarcity of purely sincere deeds does not require the slowness of their ascent to heaven, but rather their scarcity [is what it requires]. It was also read: (ya'uddūna) with the letter ya'.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 6:

﴿That﴾ is a reference to Allah, glory be to Him, in respect of His being characterized by what has been mentioned: the creation of the heavens and the earth, the establishment upon the Throne (istiwa' ala al-'arsh), the exclusivity of guardianship (wilaya) and support (nusra) in Him, and the governance of the affairs of all beings in the wondrous manner that has been mentioned. It is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is what follows it, i.e., "That One, Possessor of Supreme Majesty."

﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾: so He manages their affair as wisdom requires.

﴿The Almighty﴾: the Overpowering over His affair.

(p-81) ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ toward His servants. These two are further predicates (khabarani akharan), and in them is an indication that He, exalted is He, is bountiful in all that has been mentioned and acts with benevolence.

The Qur'an says, ﴿Who perfected everything He created﴾, and this is another predicate, or it is in the accusative as a term of praise, meaning: He made beautiful every creature He created. For no creature is created except that it is arranged in accordance with what wisdom requires and what benefit necessitates. Thus all creatures are good, although they vary between good and better, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We created man in the best of stature﴾. It has been said that He "knew how to create it" from the saying "a man's worth is what he does well (yuhsinu)", meaning he knows it well, that is, he knows it with a good knowledge, with verification and certainty.

It was also read as "khalaqahu" (his creation) in apposition of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal, a substitution in which the second term includes the first) to "kulla shay'" (everything). The pronoun refers back to the substituted term, meaning: He made the creation of everything beautiful. It has been said that it is a complete substitution (badal al-kull), with the pronoun referring to God, exalted is He. "Khalq" here means "makhluq" (creature), meaning: He made all His creatures beautiful. It has also been said that it is a second object of "ahsana" (to perfect), with the verb taken to imply the meaning of "a'ta" (to give), meaning: He gave everything its fitting creation by way of perfection and grace. It has been said that it is its first object and "kulla shay'" is its second object, with "khalq" meaning "makhluq", and its pronoun referring to God, glorified is He, with "ihsan" (perfecting) implying the meaning of "ilham" (inspiration) and "ta'rif" (making known). The meaning is: He inspired His creation with everything they need. Abu al-Baqa' said: He made His creatures know everything they need, which returns to the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾. ﴿And He began the creation of man﴾ from among all creatures ﴿from clay﴾, in a wondrous manner whose understanding baffles minds, in that He brought Adam, peace be upon him, into being with a marvelous innate nature which comprehensively contains the innate natures of all the individuals of the species in a summary way, entailing that each individual of them emerges from potentiality into actuality according to their varying readinesses, near and far, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates:

Then He made his offspring from an extract of a fluid, a base water.

Here "nasl" (offspring) means his progeny ("dhurriyyah"). It was so called because it issues forth (yanselu) and separates (yanfasilu) from him.

﴿from an extract of a fluid, a base water﴾: this is the despised (mumtahan) seminal fluid (al-maniyy).

ثُمَّ سَوّاهُ — that is, He balanced him (عدله) by perfecting his limbs in the womb and shaping them as they ought to be.

وَنَفَخَ فِيهِ مِن رُوحِهِ — He attributed it to Himself (أضافَهُ إلَيْهِ تَعالى) to honour it, and to announce that it is a wondrous creation, a marvellous handiwork, and that it has a matter (شأنًا) that bears a relation to the presence of Lordship (حضرة الربوبية). The furthest that human intellects can reach in knowing it is this degree, which is expressed sometimes by its attribution to Him, the Exalted, and sometimes by its relation to His command, the Exalted, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say, "The Spirit is by the command of my Lord."﴾

وَجَعَلَ لَكُمُ السَّمْعَ والأبْصارَ والأفْئِدَةَ — The "ja'l" (making) is creative (إبداعيّ). The "lam" (لكم) is connected to it. The fronting of the phrase before the direct object (المفعول الصريح), for the reason mentioned many times, is to give prominence to what is fronted and to create anticipation for what is delayed, together with the fact that it is somewhat lengthy, which fronting would disturb the eloquence of the noble arrangement. That is: He created those faculties for your benefit, so that you might know that they, while in themselves being magnificent blessings whose worth cannot be measured, are also means to enjoying all the other religious and worldly blessings that overflow upon you, and that you might give thanks for them by directing each of them to the purpose for which it was created: thus you perceive with your hearing the revealed verses (الآيات التنزيلية) which speak of Divine Unity and the Resurrection, with your sight the created signs (الآيات التكوينية) which bear witness to both, and you reason with your hearts to their reality. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿قَلِيلا ما تَشْكُرُونَ﴾ [little is it that you give thanks] is an explanation of their disbelief in those blessings, by way of a concluding parenthetical objection (الاعتراض التذييلي), with the meaning that "qillah" (paucity) carries the sense of negation, as what follows indicates; that is: little thanks, or for a little time do you give thanks. And in narrating the states of man from the beginning of his creation until the breathing of the spirit into him by way of the third person (الغيبة), and then narrating his states after that by way of direct address (الخطاب), which indicates his readiness for understanding and his fitness for it, there is a splendour of eloquence beyond which there is no further degree.

And they say, ﴿When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ This is a resumed statement, brought to expose their falsehoods by way of iltifat (shift in grammatical person), signalling that their not being grateful for those blessings warrants turning away from them, and that recounting their misdeeds to others is done in a manner of reproach.

﴿When we have gone astray in the earth﴾ means: we have become dust mixed with its dust such that we are not distinguished from it, or we have been lost within it through burial. It is also read (ḍalilnā), with the kasra on the lam, from the pattern of ʿalima, and (ṣalalnā), with the unpointed ṣad, from ṣalla al-laḥm (ṣalla, meaning the meat became putrid). It has been said that it comes from al-ṣalla, which is the earth, meaning: we have become of the substance of ṣalla. It is said the speaker was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and because they approved of his statement, the saying is attributed to all of them. The element governing "idhā" (when) is what is indicated by the words of God Most High, ﴿Shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾, namely "we will be resurrected," or "our creation will be renewed." The hamza (interrogative particle) serves to recall the earlier denial and to emphasise it. It is also read ("innā"), as a declarative statement, and in either case the meaning is on the emphasis of the denial, not the denial of the emphasis, as would seem obvious from the hamza being placed before "inna," since in terms of meaning it is placed after it, and its being placed before it is only because it requires initial position.

﴿Nay, but they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ is a turning away and a transition from explaining their disbelief in the resurrection to explaining what is more emphatic and more grievous than it, namely their disbelief in arriving at the final outcome, together with all the conditions and terrors they will encounter therein.

Say (this is a clarification of the truth and a rebuttal of their false claim): "The Angel of Death will take you in death (لا كَما تَزْعُمُونَ) — not as you claim, that death is a natural condition afflicting living beings by the necessity of their nature — he will seize your souls in such a way that he leaves nothing of you, or he does not leave any one of you, in the most severe and dreadful of states, including the striking of your faces and your backs."

﴿Who has been entrusted with you﴾, that is, with seizing your souls and reckoning your appointed terms.

﴿Then to your Lord you will be returned﴾, for resurrection, for reckoning and recompense.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 12:**

﴿If only you could see when the guilty ones﴾ (they are the ones who say: ﴿"Can it be that when we are lost in the earth..."﴾ ... the verse) or the class of the guilty, of whom they are part.

﴿Will hang their heads before their Lord﴾ out of shame and humiliation when their ugly deeds, which they committed in the world, become manifest.

﴿"Our Lord"﴾ meaning: they say, "Our Lord."

﴿"We have seen and heard"﴾ meaning: we have become among those who see and hear, and we have acquired the readiness to perceive the visible signs and the audible signs. Before this we were blind and deaf, unable to perceive anything.

﴿"So send us back"﴾ to the world ﴿"that we may do"﴾ righteous ﴿deeds"﴾ in accordance with what those signs require. His words, exalted is He, ﴿"Indeed we are certain"﴾ are a claim on their part to the soundness of their hearts, and to the capacity to understand the meanings of the signs and to act upon what they entail. Just as what precedes it is a claim to the soundness of the faculties of sight and hearing, as if they said: "And we have become certain, whereas before we were not understanding anything at all." They turned to the emphatic nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya al-mu'akkada, a sentence beginning with a noun and reinforced by an emphasizing particle) only to show their steadfastness in certainty and their complete eagerness for it, and all of this is in earnest appeal, hoping for a response to what they asked of (p-83) the return, though how could that be for them?

It is permissible that each of the two verbs be given a suitable object drawn from what they see and hear. In that case they witness disbelief and sins in hideous, dreadful forms, and the angels inform them that their destination is the Fire without doubt. The meaning then is: "We saw the ugliness of our deeds, which we used to see in the world as fine, and we heard that our return is to the Fire." This is the most fitting reading in light of what follows it, namely the promise of righteous deeds.

It has also been said: the meaning is "and we heard from You the confirmation of Your messengers." You know well that God's confirmation of them at that time consists in the manifestation of what the content of their reports of promise and threat amounts to, not in the announcement that they are truthful so that they might hear it. It has also been said: "and we heard the word of the messengers," i.e., we heard it with the hearing of obedience and submission.

No object is to be supplied for "tara" (you see), since the meaning is: "If there were a seeing from you at that time." Or there may be supplied something that indicates it as a complement, since "idh" (when) and the past tense are used in it. As for "law" (if only), it is considered in view of the fact that what is established in God's knowledge stands in the position of what has actually occurred. The apodosis of "law" is omitted, i.e., "you would see a dreadful matter whose extent cannot be measured." The address is to everyone who is fit for it, whoever he may be, since the purpose is to explain the completeness of their wretched state and how far its horror reaches, to the point that its strangeness and dreadfulness are not restricted to one who sees over another, but to anyone who is able to see, one who has become accustomed to witnessing wondrous things and grave calamities. Rather, everyone capable of seeing is amazed at its terror and horror. Moreover, among the reasons for the general address by intent is to show that their condition has reached such a degree of manifestness that its concealment is absolutely impossible, so that the seeing of one seer is not distinguished from another's; rather, everyone capable of seeing has a share in this address. Yet he has strayed far from the realization of the truth, because the intended purpose is to explain the completeness of the horror of their condition, as the omitted apodosis makes clear, not to explain the completeness of its manifestness, for that is presented as a matter already granted. So reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 13:

﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ is governed by a statement that is coordinated with what was implied before the Almighty's words: ﴿"Our Lord, we have seen and heard..."﴾ etc. That is: "And We say, 'Had We willed,'" that is, had Our will been connected in an active manner to giving every soul, of the righteous and the wicked souls, that by which it would be guided to faith and righteous action, We would have given it to them in this world, which is the abode of earning, and We would not have deferred it to the abode of recompense.

﴿But the word from Me has been fulfilled﴾ means: My word has preceded, when I said to Iblis, at his saying: ﴿"I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them"﴾ [Q 15:39–40], ﴿"So the truth is, and the truth I say: I will surely fill Hell with you and with those who follow you among them, all together"﴾ [Q 38:84–85]. This is what is meant by the Almighty's words: ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men, all together"﴾ [Q 32:13], as is indicated by the mention of the jinn before men. Accordingly, by the terms of that word, We did not will to give guidance universally; rather, We withheld it from the followers of Iblis, of whom you are among the number, since you directed your choice toward error through his seduction. Our will regarding the actions of servants is contingent upon their choosing it. So when you did not choose guidance and chose misguidance, We did not will to give it to you. We gave it only to those who chose it from the righteous souls, and they are the ones meant by what follows in the Almighty's words: ﴿"Only those believe in Our signs..."﴾ [Q 32:15], etc. Thus the true basis for the non-willing of giving guidance is their evil choice, not the fulfilment of the word. We restricted the will by what has passed of active connection to the actions of servants at the moment they occur, because the eternal will, insofar as it relates to what their actions will be in summary, precedes the realisation of the word of punishment; so its non-existence is not contingent upon its realisation. Its basis is rather His eternal knowledge, may He be exalted, of the turning of their choice in the future toward error and their preference for it over guidance. Had that will been meant in that respect, it would have been overtaken by its non-existence, and it would have been attached to the basis mentioned, following the method of the Almighty's words: ﴿"Had Allah known any good in them, He would have made them hear"﴾ [Q 8:23]. So whoever imagines that the meaning is: "Had We willed, We would have given every soul what We possess of grace which, had they chosen it, they would have been guided; but We did not give it to them because We knew of them their choice of disbelief and their preference for it," has confused the matters.

And the "fa'" in the Almighty's words:

﴿So taste﴾ is for the sequencing of the command to tasting (*tartib*, ordering of consequence) upon what the preceding statement, the denial of returning to the world, indicates, or upon the threat that was related.

The "bā'" (*al-bā'*, the particle of causality) in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿because you forgot the meeting of this your day﴾, is to announce that their punishment is not merely because the threat was given beforehand, but because the threat, together with a cause that necessitates it on their part, was given beforehand. It is as if it were said: "There is no return for you to the world, or even My threat: so taste, because of your forgetting the meeting of this terrible day, your abandonment of reflecting upon it, and your complete failure to prepare for it."

﴿Indeed We have forgotten you﴾, meaning: We have left you in the punishment as one who is wholly forgotten is left. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And taste the punishment of eternity because of what you used to do﴾, is a repetition for emphasis and intensification. The specification of the omitted object of the tasting, and the indication that its cause is not merely the aforementioned forgetting but that there are other causes from the various kinds of disbelief and sins in which they persisted in the world, and the non-arrangement of all of them in a single series, is to draw attention to the independent sufficiency of each of them in necessitating the punishment. And [there is] in the obscuring of what is tasted at first, and its clarification second, through the repetition of the command and the insertion of the resumptive clause (*isti'nāf*), which indicates complete wrath between them, [a sign] of the intensification of vengeance against them that is not hidden. And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 15:

﴿Only those believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them, fall down prostrate and glorify the praise of their Lord, and they are not arrogant.﴾

Here "Innama" (only, exclusively) introduces a resumptive sentence (istinaf) that serves to establish that they do not deserve to be granted guidance, and to indicate, through the restrictive construction (qasr) that specifies who deserves it, that even if it were granted to them they would not believe. It is as if it were said: "You do not believe in Our signs, and you do not act upon what they require with righteous deeds; and even if We returned you to the world, as you claim, you would revert to what you were forbidden," in accordance with the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden﴾. "Only those believe in them who, when they are reminded of them" — that is, who are admonished by them.

﴿They fall down prostrate﴾ — he hastens to it (athir dhi athir) without hesitation or delay, let alone postponing it until they witness what its promise and threat have spoken of. That is, they fall upon their faces.

﴿And glorify the praise of their Lord﴾ — that is, they declare Him far exalted at that moment above everything unbefitting Him, among which is inability to resurrect, while joining that glorification with praise of Him, the Exalted, for His bounties, the greatest of which is guidance through the granting of the signs and enabling them to be guided by them. The address by the title of Lordship (rububiyya), by way of iltifat (shift from third to second/first person address), together with the attribution to their pronoun, indicates the reason for the glorification and praise, and that they perform both while mindful of His Lordship over them, may He be exalted.

﴿And they are not arrogant﴾ — that is, while they are humbled before Him, the Exalted, they are not arrogant regarding what they have done of prostration, glorification and praise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 16:

﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾ i.e., they turn away and withdraw (tanabbu wa-tatanahha).

﴿from the couches﴾ i.e., the bedding and the places of sleep. The clause is a new sentence (mustaʼnafah) explaining the rest of their excellent qualities, namely that they are the ones who perform the tahajjud (night prayer, supererogatory vigil) at night. Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It was revealed concerning us, the company of the Ansar: we used to pray the Maghrib and would not return to our homes until we prayed the ʽIshaʼ with the Prophet ﷺ." And also from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "It was revealed concerning some of the companions of the Prophet ﷺ who used to pray from the Maghrib prayer until the ʽIshaʼ prayer, and that is the prayer of the awwabin (those who turn often to Allah)." This is the view of Abu Hazim and Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, and it is also reported from Ibn ʽAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. ʽAta said: "They are those who do not sleep until they have prayed the final ʽIshaʼ and the Fajr in congregation."

The well-known view is that what is meant is the night prayer (salat al-layl), and this is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, Malik, al-Awza'i and a group of others, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The best fasting after the month of Ramadan is the month of Allah, al-Muharram, and the best prayer after the obligatory prayer is the night prayer." And from the Prophet ﷺ in explanation of it: "The standing of the servant in the night (qiyam al-ʽabd min al-layl)." And from him ﷺ: "When Allah gathers the first and the last, a caller will call out with a voice that makes all creatures hear: 'The people of the gathering will know today who is most deserving of honour.' Then he returns and calls: 'Let those stand whose sides used to forsake their beds.' They stand, and they are few. Then he returns and calls: 'Let those stand who used to praise Allah in ease and in hardship.' They stand, and they are few. They are all sent off to Paradise, and then the rest of the people are called to account."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿calling upon their Lord﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "their sides", i.e., calling upon Him, exalted is He, continually; ﴿in fear﴾ of His wrath, His punishment, and the non-acceptance of their worship, ﴿and in hope﴾ of His mercy.

﴿And from what We have provided them﴾ of wealth ﴿they spend﴾ in the ways of righteousness and good deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 17:

﴿No soul knows﴾ of the souls, neither an angel brought near nor a prophet sent, let alone others besides them.

﴿What has been concealed for them﴾ i.e., for those whose sublime qualities have been enumerated.

﴿of comfort for the eyes﴾ of that which their eyes are comforted by. The Prophet (ﷺ) said that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." This is beyond what you have witnessed. Recite, if you wish: ﴿No soul knows what has been concealed for them of comfort for the eyes﴾. It was also read as (ma ukhfiya lahum) and (ma nukhfi lahum) and (ma akhfaytu lahum) in the first person form, and (ma akhfa lahum) in the active voice, whose agent is Allah, glorified is He. It was also read as (qurrati a'yun), owing to the variety of its kinds. The verb "ya'lam" (know) here means "ma'rifa" (recognition, knowledge), and "ma" is either a relative pronoun or an interrogative, with the verb suspended from its operation (ta'liq).

﴿As a reward for what they used to do﴾ i.e., they are rewarded a reward, or what has been concealed for them is for the recompense of what they used to do in the world of righteous deeds. It has been said: these people concealed their deeds, so Allah, exalted is He, concealed their reward.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 18:

﴿Is he who is a believer like him who is a defiant transgressor?﴾ That is: after the clear disparity between the two has become apparent, could it be imagined that the believer, whose virtuous attributes have been related, is like the defiant transgressor, whose conditions have been mentioned?

﴿They are not equal﴾. The explicit statement of this, together with the implication of denial, is to negate any resemblance altogether, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, so that the detailed account that follows may be built upon it. The plural form is used in view of the meaning of "man" (min), just as the singular was used earlier in view of its wording. And His Exalted saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 19:

﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them are the Gardens of Refuge﴾ is a detailing of the ranks of the two groups in the Hereafter, after mentioning their conditions in this world. The garden (jannah) is attributed to "al-ma'wa" (the refuge) because it is the true refuge, whereas this world is merely a dwelling that one will inevitably depart from. It has also been said: "al-ma'wa" is a garden among the gardens. Whatever the case, it is not far-fetched that there is in it a symbolic allusion to what was mentioned of their withdrawing their sides from their beds (p-86), which are their refuge in this world. ﴿Nuzulan﴾, meaning: a reward. Literally, it is what is prepared for the guest of food and drink, and its accusative placement is in the sense of a circumstantial state (hal).

﴿Bima kanu ya'malun﴾: because of the righteous deeds they performed in the world, or "bi-a'malihim" (by their deeds).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 20:

﴿As for those who defied (fasaqu)﴾ i.e., they went out of obedience.

﴿Then their refuge (ma'wahum)﴾ i.e., their shelter and their dwelling.

﴿Is the Fire﴾ in place of the Gardens of Refuge (jannat al-ma'wa) for the believers. ﴿Whenever they wish to get out of it, they will be returned to it﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) to explain how the Fire becomes their refuge. It is related that the flame of the Fire strikes them, so they rise up to its levels, until, when they come near its gate and wish to get out of it, the flame strikes them and they plunge down to its bottom, and so it is done to them forever. The word "fi" (in) indicates that they are settled in it; the return is only from some of its levels to others.

﴿And it will be said to them﴾ as a rebuke to them and an increase in their rage.

﴿Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾ i.e., the punishment of the Fire.

﴿Persistently (in the world)﴾ — translated as: you used to deny persistently in the world.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 21:

﴿And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment﴾, i.e., the punishment of this world. This is what they were afflicted with: the years of famine seven years long, the killing, and the captivity.

﴿Short of the greater punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Hereafter.

﴿So that perhaps﴾, perhaps those who witness it while they are alive ﴿will return﴾, i.e., will repent of disbelief. It is narrated that al-Walid ibn 'Uqba boasted against 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) on the day of Badr, and then these verses were revealed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 22:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turns away from them?﴾ This is a general statement about the state of one who confronts the signs of God, Exalted is He, with aversion, following the explanation of the state of one who confronts them with prostration, glorification, and praise. The word "thumma" (then) here indicates the remoteness of turning away from them by reason, given their utmost clarity and their guidance to the happiness of both abodes. As in the verse of the Hamasa:

"None removes the calamity except the son of a free woman, who sees the pangs of death and then visits them."

That is: he is more unjust than every unjust person. Although the structure of the expression is built on negating greater injustice without addressing the negation of other faults, this has been discussed repeatedly.

﴿Indeed, We take vengeance upon the criminals﴾ That is: upon every one who is characterized by criminality, even if his crime is minor.

﴿Vengeance﴾ So how about one who is more unjust than every unjust person, and more evil in crime than every criminal?

(Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 32, verse 23)

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾ That is, the Torah. It is expressed by the generic name (ism al-jins) to establish the affinity between it and the Furqan, and to draw attention to the fact that the giving of it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is like the giving of it to Moses, peace be upon him.

﴿So be not in doubt about meeting him﴾ About meeting the Book, which is the Furqan, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed you receive the Qur'an﴾. The meaning is: We gave Moses a Book like what We gave you, and We made him meet revelation like what We made you meet. So do not be in doubt that you have met its like and its counterpart. It was also said: "about meeting Moses the Book," or "about your meeting Moses." And from him (ﷺ): "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I saw Moses, a man of brown complexion, tall, and curly-haired, as though he were one of the men of Shanu'ah." ﴿And We made it﴾, that is, (p-87) the Book which We gave Moses, ﴿a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾. It was said: no descendant of Isma'il worshipped by what is in the Torah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 24:

﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding﴾ their remnant (baqiyyatahum) by the wisdom and rulings contained within the folds of the Book (tadaʿif al-kitab) to the path of truth; or they guide them to what it contains of the religion of God and His laws.

﴿By Our command﴾ to them to do so, or by Our granting them success in it (tawfiq).

﴿When they were patient﴾ This is "lamma" which carries the meaning of a conditional (jaza'), like the example: "I was good to you when (lamma) you came to me." The pronoun refers to the leaders, its implied sense being "When they were patient, We made them leaders." Or it is an adverb of time meaning "when" (al-hin), i.e., We made them leaders at the time they were patient. What is meant is their patience in the hardships of acts of obedience and in enduring trials in supporting the religion, or their patience in renouncing this world. It has also been read as (limā ṣabarū), meaning: because of their patience.

﴿And they were, of Our signs﴾ that are within the folds of the Book.

﴿certain (yuqinun)﴾ because of their deep and sustained reflection upon them. The meaning is: Thus We shall surely make the Book which We gave you a guidance for your community, and We shall surely make from among them leaders guiding with the like of that guidance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, your Lord – He is the one who will decide⟩ i.e., He will judge (yaqdi).

﴿between them⟩ It has been said: between the prophets and their nations; and it has been said: between the believers and the polytheists (mushrikin).

﴿on the Day of Resurrection⟩ and He will distinguish between the righteous (muhiqq) and the falsehood-follower (mubtil) ﴿concerning that about which they used to differ⟩ of matters of the religion (din).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 26:

﴿Has it not guided them?﴾ The *hamzah* (interrogative particle) here is for denial (*inkar*), and the *waw* is for conjunction (*'atf*), coordinating with an implied element that the context requires. The verb *al-hidayah* (guiding) is either of the type of "so-and-so gives," where the intent is the occurrence of the act itself without regard to its object, or it carries the meaning of clarifying (*al-tabyin*), with the object omitted. The subject is what is indicated by His words, exalted is He, ﴿how many We destroyed﴾, meaning: they were heedless. Either the guiding was not done for them, or the great number of Our destructions of the generations before them did not make clear to them the outcome of their affair, such as ʿAd, Thamud, and the people of Lut. It is also recited as *nahdi lahum* (﴿We guide them﴾) with the *nun* of majesty (*nun al-'azamah*). It is permissible that, according to the first recitation as well, the subject be His own pronoun, so that His words ﴿how many We destroyed﴾ ... etc. constitute a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) explaining the manner of His guiding.

﴿They walk in their dwellings﴾: that is, they pass through their marketplaces over their homes and lands, and they observe the traces of their destruction. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in "for them." It is also recited as *yumashshun* (with intensive doubling), for intensification (*lil-takthir*).

﴿Indeed, in that﴾: that is, in what has been mentioned of Our great destruction of the arrogant, bygone nations, or in their dwellings ﴿are signs﴾, great in themselves and numerous in their count.

﴿Will they not then hear?﴾ These signs, with the hearing of reflection and admonition.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 27:

﴿Have they not seen that We drive the water to the barren land﴾. That is: the land whose vegetation has been cut off (juriza nabatuha), i.e., cut down and entirely removed. It has also been said that al-Ardh al-Juruz is the name of a place in Yemen.

﴿Then We bring forth thereby﴾ from that land,

﴿crops of which their cattle eat﴾. That is: from that crop, such as chaff (tibn), green fodder (qasil), leaves, and some of the particular grains specific to them. It is also read as (ya'kulu) with the letter ya.

﴿and themselves﴾, such as the grains that humans subsist on, and fruits.

﴿Will they not then see?﴾ (p-88) That is: will they not look, so that they see that and draw inference from it regarding the perfection of His power, may He be exalted, and His bounty?

"And they say, [the Muslims used to say: God will grant us victory over the polytheists, or He will decide between us and them. And the people of Mecca, when they heard this, would say, by way of haste, denying and mocking: ﴿When is this victory?﴾ That is: the help (victory), or the decision by judgment.]

﴿If you are truthful﴾ in your claim that God, exalted is He, will help you, or will decide between us and you."

**﴿Say﴾** — as a rebuke to them and to establish the truth.

**﴿On the Day of Victory, the faith of those who disbelieved will not benefit them, nor will they be given respite﴾** — "The Day of Victory" is the Day of Resurrection, and it is the Day of Decision (al-Fasl) between the believers and their enemies, and the Day of their victory over them. It has also been said that it is the Day of Badr. And from Mujahid and al-Hasan: it is the Day of the Conquest of Mecca. The departure from matching the answer to the apparent form of their question is to alert that this is not something that should be asked about, since it is a clear matter that needs no informing; likewise their faith and their seeking respite on that day. What really requires explanation is the non-benefit of that faith and the absence of respite. It is as if it was said: "Do not hasten; soon you will believe and your faith will not benefit you, and you will seek respite and you will not be given respite." This is evident according to the first interpretation. As for the last two interpretations, the relative clause refers to those who were killed on that day, not to all the disbelievers, as in the first interpretation. How could it be otherwise, when faith benefited the freed captives (al-Tulaqa') on the Day of Conquest, and some people who believed on the Day of Badr?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 32, verse 30:

﴿So turn away from them﴾, and do not care about their denial, ﴿and wait﴾ for victory over them and their destruction, ﴿indeed they are waiting﴾. It has been said: that is, waiting for the triumph over you, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So wait, indeed we are with you among those who wait﴾. But the more apparent view is that it is said: they are waiting for their own destruction, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of cloud﴾... the verse. Close to this is what has been said: ﴿and wait﴾ for Our punishment, ﴿indeed they are waiting﴾, for their hastening mentioned above and their persistence in the disbelief and sins they are upon is, in ruling, their waiting for the punishment that will inevitably follow from it. It was also read in the passive form (ṣīghat al-maf'ūl), meaning: they are deserving that their destruction be awaited; or, ﴿indeed the angels are waiting for it﴾.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Alif Lam Mim, the Revelation (tanzil), and Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion (tabaraka alladhi bi-yadihi al-mulk), he will be given a reward as if he had enlivened the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr)."

And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Alif Lam Mim, the Revelation, in his house, the Shaytan will not enter it for three days."
